questions.question: Why can't a vector be fully described by a single number?
questions.solution: A vector carries TWO pieces of information: magnitude (how much) and direction (which way). A single number discards the direction — and direction changes the outcome of every vector operation (adding, projecting, rotating). Vectors exist precisely because some quantities need both.

questions.question: What does multiplying a vector by −2 do, and why does the result stay parallel to the original?
questions.solution: −2 doubles the magnitude and REVERSES the direction (opposite way along the same line). Scaling never changes the LINE the vector lies on — only length and sense. Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other.

questions.question: A force of 10 N acts at 60° to the direction of motion over 5 m. Use the dot product to find the work done and interpret the cosθ factor.
questions.solution: W = F·d = |F||d|cosθ = 10 × 5 × cos60° = 25 J. cos60° = ½ is the fraction of the force that acts ALONG the motion — only the projected component does work. The perpendicular half contributes nothing. The dot product is the projection machine.

questions.question: What are the direction cosines of a vector, and why do their squares sum to 1?
questions.solution: They are the cosines of the angles the vector makes with the x, y, z axes — equivalently the components of the unit vector along it. Unit-vector components satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1 by Pythagoras in 3D. Direction cosines are a vector's direction written as three numbers.

questions.question: Why does the midpoint of AB have position vector (a + b)/2?
questions.solution: The midpoint divides AB in ratio 1:1, and the section formula gives r = (1·a + 1·b)/(1+1) = (a+b)/2 — the average of the endpoint vectors. Geometrically: from the origin, the midpoint sits halfway along the vector sum. Averages of position vectors are the vector way to do coordinate geometry.

questions.concept: Why the dot product is a scalar
questions.question: a·b returns a single number while a×b returns a vector. What is each product measuring?
questions.solution: The dot product measures ALIGNMENT — the component of one vector along the other, a·b = |a||b|cosθ. That is a quantity with no direction, so it is a scalar. The cross product measures the AREA/rotation swept, |a||b|sinθ, which has both magnitude and an orientation (the normal), so it is a vector. One product collapses direction; the other creates it.

questions.question: Why does the vanishing dot product identify perpendicularity, and why does the vanishing cross product identify parallelism?
questions.solution: a·b = |a||b|cosθ vanishes when cosθ = 0, i.e. θ = 90° — no component along each other. a×b = |a||b|sinθ vanishes when sinθ = 0, i.e. θ = 0° or 180° — no area swept between them. Each product vanishes for the configuration it cannot measure: the dot for perpendicular, the cross for parallel. Zero is informative.

questions.concept: Why the scalar triple product gives volume
questions.question: Explain why |a·(b×c)| equals the volume of the parallelepiped formed by a, b and c.
questions.solution: b×c is a vector whose magnitude is the AREA of the base parallelogram and whose direction is normal to that base. Dotting with a projects a onto that normal, giving the height. Area × height = volume, with the absolute value removing orientation. The triple product factors volume into base area and perpendicular height.
